---
title: "Projects are folders, files are the truth"
subtitle: "How Flux saves, why nothing is ever trapped, and how humans and agents share one project safely"
---

Flux's deepest design decision is that a project is **just a folder**, and everything in it is
an ordinary, readable file. Your manuscript is a plain-text Quarto file. Your bibliography is a
BibTeX file. Your figures and slides are JSON you can open in any editor. There is no database,
no proprietary container, no cloud copy — which means no lock-in, easy backups, clean version
control, and a project you can inspect, script, or hand to an AI agent with nothing more than a
file path. ([The full folder tour](../reference/project-layout.qmd).)

# Source files and derived files

Every file in a project is one of three kinds:

- **Yours to edit freely** — `paper/**/*.qmd` (documents; `manuscript/` remains supported), `references/library.bib` (the
  project's citations), and `plots/` (where your analysis code drops its output). These are the
  source of truth; edit them in Flux, in another editor, or from a script — all equivalent.
- **App-managed** — `fig/` (figure compositions) and `slides/` (decks). These are readable
  JSON, but they're maintained by the app and its commands so that indexes, captions, and
  cross-references stay coherent. Look inside whenever you like; make changes through Flux (or
  the [`flux` command line](../reference/cli.qmd)) rather than by hand.
- **Derived** — rendered figures (`fig/renders/`), compiled output (`exports/`), and various
  caches. Everything derived is rebuildable: if it's stale or missing, Flux regenerates it.
  Derived files are safe to leave out of backups and version control.

The same division applies to [3D models](../modes/figure.qmd#3d-models-and-3d-fluxplots).
Your analysis writes a GLB mesh and optional semantic manifest to `plots/`. Flux keeps an
accepted copy in `fig/assets/`, and stores its camera, shape weights and part restyles in
the composition. Mesh posters under `fig/renders/model3d/` are a derived cache. Keep the
accepted GLB when sharing or backing up the project; the PNG cache can be rebuilt.

# Saving: you don't

Flux autosaves as you work. A file replacement writes and flushes a temporary file before
renaming it. Figure and Deck publication also retain a recovery journal containing the prior
bytes while assets, compositions, captions and project registration change. On reopening,
an interrupted generation is restored when the files still match the recorded versions.
Unexpected external edits stop recovery and retain the record for reconciliation.

Edits still waiting for autosave have not reached disk. A failed save leaves the editor dirty;
resolve its error before closing. These local transactions do not make a cloud-sync snapshot
or an entire project backup atomic.

What you do get is **deep undo**: **Ctrl+Z** in the editors walks back through your editing
history, including edits an agent made live while you watched.

# When someone else edits a file

Because the files are ordinary, other programs will sometimes write them — your own editor, a
script regenerating a plot, an AI agent revising the manuscript. Flux watches the project and
handles this without drama:

- If you have **no unsaved edits** in the affected file, the app quietly live-reloads it. A
  regenerated plot hot-swaps into your figure in place, keeping the styling you did on top.
- If you **were mid-edit**, Flux shows a banner. **Reload theirs** adopts the supported disk
  version. Figure **Overwrite with mine** saves the current figures **and captions**, first
  preserving both versions in `.meta/figure-conflicts/`. This also handles a deleted or corrupt
  canvas/index using the last complete editor state. A newer format or unreadable file refuses
  overwrite and keeps your edits dirty. Read the error before choosing another action.

# Sharing a project with agents

The same folder is the agents' workspace, and two mechanisms keep the coexistence safe:

- **Locks.** While you're actively mid-edit, the app holds an advisory lock; an agent command
  arriving at that moment defers with a polite "locked" message and retries, instead of
  clobbering the state under your cursor.
- **The journal.** Every write to the project is logged in `.meta/journal.ndjson` — who (you,
  which agent), what, and when. If something looks different than you left it, the journal says
  exactly what happened.

Start with [Working with AI agents](../agents/connect.qmd), maintain
[your context](../agents/context.qmd), and use [annotations and Inbox](../agents/annotations.qmd)
to point out work and follow replies.

# Version control and portability

Projects are deliberately git-friendly: plain text and JSON, stable keys, small diffs. Committing
a project works exactly as you'd expect, and the derived directories are the only things worth
ignoring. A project is also **self-contained** — its `references/library.bib` holds real copies
of the entries it cites (not pointers into your [machine library](library-and-fluxlib.qmd)), so
zipping the folder, cloning it, or opening it on another machine just works.
